medium.resumo: From digital products and freelance services to niche websites, prompt packs and subscriptions — with workflows, examples and ready-to-use…
medium.conteudo_html:
From digital products and freelance services to niche websites, prompt packs and subscriptions — with workflows, examples and ready-to-use AI prompts.

In Part 1 of this series, we explored five ways to build an AI-assisted digital business:

  1. Digital products
  2. Freelance services
  3. Niche websites
  4. Prompt packs
  5. Subscription-based resources

Want to Build An Online Business with AI?

We also discussed an important principle: a business should begin with a problem people want solved, not with an AI tool you are excited to try.

Now comes the practical part.

You have selected an audience, identified a problem and chosen a business model. How do you turn that idea into an actual offer?

Let’s say you have decided to serve independent fitness coaches. You have discovered that many struggle to create consistent social media content while managing their clients and daily operations.

You could create a downloadable content planner, offer a monthly content-writing service, build a niche website, sell a collection of AI prompts or launch a monthly resource membership.

The audience is similar. The business models are different. And each requires a different creation process.

This article walks through all five.

The aim is not to build five businesses simultaneously. It is to understand the workflow behind each model so you can choose one and create a credible first version.

1. Building a digital product: Turn knowledge into a useful resource

Digital products are often one of the easiest models to prototype because you can begin with a relatively small deliverable.

You do not need to write a 100-page ebook or create an elaborate online course.

A focused checklist, workbook, planner or practical guide can be a perfectly reasonable first product — provided it solves a real problem.

Step 1: Define the transformation

Before opening ChatGPT or Claude, complete this sentence:

“My product helps [specific audience] move from [current problem] to [desired outcome] through [specific resource].”

Example:

“My product helps independent fitness coaches move from inconsistent social media posting to a more organized monthly content routine through a customizable content-planning workbook.”

This sentence becomes your product’s foundation.

It tells you what to include and, equally importantly, what to leave out.

Step 2: Decide what the buyer should receive

For the fitness coach workbook, a useful first version might contain:

  • A monthly content-planning calendar.
  • A weekly content theme planner.
  • A list of educational post ideas.
  • A caption-writing worksheet.
  • A simple content tracking sheet.
  • A review page to identify what worked.

Notice that this is more useful than a document containing 50 generic social media tips.

The buyer receives something they can actually use.

A practical product structure

You can adapt this structure for many other topics.

A budgeting workbook might include an expense tracker, monthly budget planner and savings goals worksheet. A job-search guide might include an application tracker, interview preparation sheet and resume checklist.

Step 3: Use AI to develop the structure

Rather than asking AI to write an entire product in one go, use it to develop the product section by section.

Ready-to-use prompt: Product outline

Act as an experienced instructional designer and digital
product developer.
I want to create a practical digital product.
Target audience: [Describe audience]
Problem: [Describe the problem]
Desired outcome: [What should the buyer achieve?]
Product format: [Workbook / guide / checklist / planner]
Create a detailed product outline.
For every section:
1. Explain its purpose.
2. Identify the information the buyer needs.
3. Suggest practical exercises or worksheets.
4. Include examples where useful.
5. Avoid unnecessary theory and repetition.
The product must be actionable and suitable for
someone who is new to the subject.
Do not invent statistics, research findings or
professional credentials.

Review the outline before asking AI to draft the content.

If the outline is too broad, narrow it. If it includes sections that do not contribute to the promised outcome, remove them.

Step 4: Draft, edit and improve

AI can help create first drafts, examples, instructions and worksheet content.

But the first draft is not the finished product.

Use this process:

  1. Generate one section at a time.
  2. Check whether the advice is accurate.
  3. Remove generic or repetitive content.
  4. Add practical examples.
  5. Simplify confusing explanations.
  6. Check that worksheets are actually usable.
  7. Read the entire product as if you were the customer.

Ready-to-use prompt: Improve a draft

Act as a professional editor and practical learning
resource developer.
Review the following draft for a digital product.
Your job is to:
- Remove repetition and generic advice.
- Improve clarity and readability.
- Identify unsupported or vague claims.
- Replace abstract suggestions with actionable steps.
- Add examples where they improve understanding.
- Check whether the content delivers the stated outcome.
Do not invent facts or claim that unverified methods
are scientifically proven.
Preserve useful information and explain any gaps
that need human review.
Draft:
[Paste your section]

If your product covers health, finance, law or another specialist area, obtain appropriate expert review rather than relying on AI to validate professional advice.

Step 5: Design and package the product

Once the content is ready, turn it into a polished resource.

Tools such as Canva, Google Docs or presentation software can help you create:

  • A professional cover.
  • Consistent headings and typography.
  • Readable tables and worksheets.
  • Page numbers and section dividers.
  • A clear final action page.

Keep the design appropriate to the subject. A children’s activity workbook should look different from a professional business toolkit.

Export the final product as a PDF when that format suits the buyer’s needs.

Before publishing, check every page. Look for broken formatting, unreadable text, incorrect links, missing pages and worksheets that are difficult to print or complete.

Step 6: Prepare the offer

A product is not ready for sale simply because the file is complete.

You also need to explain its value.

A product listing should answer:

  • Who is this for?
  • What problem does it address?
  • What exactly is included?
  • How does the buyer use it?
  • What makes it useful?
  • What should the buyer expect after purchasing?

For example:

Product: The Fitness Coach Monthly Content Planner

Description: A practical planning workbook for independent fitness coaches who want to organize their social media content without starting from scratch every week.

Includes: Monthly calendar, weekly theme planner, post idea worksheet, caption planner and content review tracker.

Format: Downloadable PDF.

You can use a digital storefront such as Gumroad to host and sell a downloadable product. The original guide that inspired this series also covers product listings, titles, descriptions, pricing and positioning. The important lesson is to make the offer clear before worrying about sophisticated marketing.

Your first milestone: Create one complete, usable digital product and prepare a product page that accurately describes it.

2. Building a freelance service: Turn a skill into a client offer

Freelancing is different from selling a downloadable product.

Here, the customer pays you to perform a task or deliver a result.

AI can help you work more efficiently, but your service must offer something beyond simply passing an instruction to ChatGPT.

Let’s continue with our fitness coach example.

The coach needs regular social media content but does not have enough time to plan and write it.

You could offer a monthly content package.

Step 1: Choose one service

Avoid starting with a long list of unrelated services.

Choose one task you can deliver reliably.

Possible examples:

A focused service is easier to explain, demonstrate and improve.

Step 2: Define the deliverables

A weak service offer sounds like this:

“I provide AI content services.”

A more useful offer sounds like this:

“I create a monthly social media content package for independent fitness coaches, including 12 post drafts, four educational captions and a content calendar.”

Now the client knows what they are paying for.

Define the scope carefully:

  • Number of deliverables.
  • Expected turnaround time.
  • Number of revisions.
  • Information required from the client.
  • What is excluded from the package.
  • How final files will be delivered.

This prevents misunderstandings later.

Step 3: Build a repeatable production workflow

Suppose you are writing social media content for a fitness coach.

Your workflow could look like this:

  1. Understand the client’s audience and services.
  2. Collect brand guidelines and relevant information.
  3. Plan monthly content themes.
  4. Draft individual posts with AI assistance.
  5. Check claims and subject-specific information.
  6. Edit the tone and improve the writing.
  7. Deliver the final content for client review.

AI should support your process, not invent client credentials, testimonials, results or professional claims.

Step 4: Use AI to create a first draft

Ready-to-use prompt: Social media content package

Act as a professional social media content strategist.
I am preparing a content package for a client.
Business type: [Describe business]
Target audience: [Describe audience]
Main services: [List services]
Brand tone: [Professional / Friendly / Educational]
Platform: [Instagram / LinkedIn / Other]
Content objective: [Educate / Engage / Generate enquiries]
Create a proposed content calendar with:
- 12 post ideas.
- A suggested content theme for each post.
- A short explanation of the audience problem addressed.
- A suggested call to action.
Avoid repetitive topics, exaggerated claims and
unsupported promises.
Do not invent client results, testimonials or credentials.

After generating the calendar, select the ideas that best match the client’s actual business.

Then create individual posts, review them and make them sound natural.

Step 5: Create a sample portfolio

You need something that demonstrates your ability.

You can create three sample projects:

Sample 1: A monthly social media calendar for a hypothetical fitness coach.

Sample 2: A short educational newsletter for a fictional wellness business.

Sample 3: A set of product descriptions for a hypothetical online store.

Label these as sample or concept projects. Do not present fictional work as paid client experience.

A small portfolio that demonstrates quality is more useful than a long list of services you cannot confidently deliver.

Step 6: Package and price the service

Start by calculating how much time the service requires.

For example, imagine your monthly content package takes:

If you decide your target working rate is ₹800 per hour, the starting calculation is:

5 × ₹800 = ₹4,000.

This is an illustrative pricing exercise, not a market-rate recommendation. Your actual price must account for client expectations, complexity, experience, revisions, overhead and competition.

Avoid pricing only by the number of words or posts. The value of the work and the time required both matter.

Step 7: Prepare a client pitch

A simple outreach message should explain the problem you can help solve and the service you offer.

Example:

Hi [Name],
I came across your fitness coaching page and noticed
that you share useful information with your audience.
I help independent fitness coaches organize their
monthly social media content.
I have prepared a sample content calendar showing
how educational posts, practical tips and engagement
content could be planned across a month.
Would you be interested in taking a look?
Best,
[Your Name]

Personalize your message. Avoid sending identical mass messages or making claims about results you cannot substantiate.

Your first milestone: Create one clearly defined service, prepare three sample deliverables and build a simple portfolio.

3. Building a niche website: Turn useful information into an audience asset

A niche website takes a different approach.

Instead of selling a single resource or providing a service, you build a focused collection of useful content for a particular audience.

This model requires consistency. Its purpose is to develop a destination that people can discover, use and return to.

Let’s build around the same audience: independent fitness coaches.

Step 1: Define the website’s focus

A broad website about fitness would be difficult to differentiate.

A more focused concept might be:

The Independent Fitness Coach Toolkit

Its purpose would be to help fitness professionals manage their content, clients and everyday business activities.

Potential content categories:

  • Marketing and content planning.
  • Client onboarding and retention.
  • Business productivity.
  • Digital tools and AI workflows.
  • Templates and downloadable resources.

The narrower focus gives the website a recognizable identity.

Step 2: Build a content map

Do not start by asking AI to generate 100 article titles.

Start by organizing the subject into connected content areas.

Example content map

This structure helps you develop a coherent website instead of a collection of unrelated articles.

Step 3: Research what the audience wants to know

Explore questions from relevant online communities, discussions and search suggestions.

Look for repeated questions such as:

  • How do I get more clients?
  • What should I post on Instagram?
  • How do I organize new client information?
  • How can I manage my weekly content?
  • Which tools help with everyday business tasks?

Turn those questions into article ideas.

Ready-to-use prompt: Niche content planner

Act as a content strategist for a focused niche website.
Website topic: [Topic]
Target audience: [Audience]
Main audience problems: [List problems]
Create a 30-article content plan organized into
3 to 5 connected categories.
For each article provide:
1. A clear, specific title.
2. The reader's main question or problem.
3. The practical value of the article.
4. Suggested examples, templates or resources.
5. How it connects to the other articles.
Avoid duplicate topics and generic AI-generated
article ideas.
Prioritize usefulness over publishing volume.

Review the ideas before building your publishing schedule.

Step 4: Develop an article production workflow

A repeatable workflow might look like this:

  1. Select one audience question.
  2. Define what the article should help the reader accomplish.
  3. Gather reliable information.
  4. Create an outline.
  5. Draft the article.
  6. Check facts and examples.
  7. Edit for clarity and usefulness.
  8. Add relevant visuals, links or downloadable resources.
  9. Publish and review reader response.

AI can assist at several stages, but it should not be used to manufacture expertise or fill the website with articles that offer nothing new.

Ready-to-use prompt: Article outline

Act as an experienced niche website content editor.
Article topic: [Topic]
Target reader: [Audience]
Reader's main problem: [Problem]
Desired outcome: [Outcome]
Create a detailed article outline.
Include:
- A useful introduction.
- Clear sections and subheadings.
- Step-by-step explanations where appropriate.
- Practical examples.
- Common mistakes.
- A conclusion with a useful next step.
Avoid filler, repetitive sections and unsupported claims.
Do not invent research, statistics or personal experiences.

Step 5: Decide how the website could earn revenue

A niche website can support several business models.

These routes are not interchangeable. They require different levels of audience trust, traffic and commercial intent.

For example, a website about fitness-coach business operations might eventually sell a client onboarding workbook or recommend relevant business tools.

The important thing is that monetization should fit the audience’s needs.

Step 6: Build a manageable publishing plan

You do not need to publish every day.

Start with a realistic schedule, such as one or two useful articles per week, depending on your available time and research requirements.

Focus on building a small collection of genuinely useful articles before expanding the site.

Your first milestone: Define the website, create a content map and prepare your first five well-researched article outlines.

4. Building a prompt pack: Turn repeatable tasks into a packaged workflow

Prompt packs are one of the more accessible ways to experiment with AI-assisted digital products.

However, there is a difference between collecting prompts and developing a useful prompt product.

A collection of random instructions is easy to generate. A tested workflow that helps a particular audience complete a recurring task is more valuable.

Let’s create a prompt pack for independent fitness coaches.

Step 1: Identify recurring tasks

Start by listing tasks the audience performs repeatedly.

For fitness coaches, these might include:

  • Creating educational social media posts.
  • Drafting client welcome messages.
  • Preparing weekly newsletters.
  • Writing service descriptions.
  • Brainstorming content themes.
  • Creating client feedback questions.

Choose one narrow category for your first pack.

For example:

AI Content Creation Prompts for Independent Fitness Coaches

This gives the product a clear purpose.

Step 2: Organize prompts by workflow

A useful collection could be divided into five sections:

The buyer should be able to find the right prompt without searching through an unorganized document.

Step 3: Build prompts with clear instructions

A strong prompt generally needs more than a role description.

It should provide context, define the task and explain the expected output.

Consider this example.

Basic prompt:

“Write an Instagram post about healthy eating.”

This is vague. It does not specify the audience, purpose, tone or type of output.

Improved prompt:

Act as a health and fitness content writer.
Create an educational Instagram caption for
a fitness coach.
Topic: [Insert topic]
Target audience: [Insert audience]
Main takeaway: [Insert takeaway]
Tone: Friendly, clear and encouraging.
Structure:
1. An opening hook.
2. A simple explanation.
3. Three practical suggestions.
4. A short concluding thought.
5. A relevant call to action.
Avoid medical claims, exaggerated promises
and unsupported nutritional advice.
Keep the language easy to understand.

This prompt provides context and a defined output structure.

Step 4: Test every prompt

This is where your product starts becoming more than a prompt collection.

Test the same prompt with different inputs.

For example:

  • A coach serving beginners.
  • A coach serving experienced athletes.
  • A coach specializing in home workouts.

Observe whether the prompt produces relevant, useful results.

Record:

  • What worked?
  • What was unclear?
  • Which instructions were ignored?
  • What information did the user need to provide?
  • What should be improved?

Do not claim a prompt is tested or reliable if you have not actually tested it.

Step 5: Create a prompt testing worksheet

Use my simple table while developing the pack.

You can rate each result from 1 to 5 for relevance, clarity and usefulness.

The score is an internal quality-control aid, not proof of guaranteed results.

Step 6: Package the collection

A practical prompt pack should include:

  • A clear introduction.
  • Instructions for using the prompts.
  • A categorized prompt library.
  • Customization guidance.
  • Sample inputs and outputs.
  • Tips for improving results.
  • Limitations and review reminders.

You can deliver it as a PDF, an organized digital document or another convenient format.

You can also explore selling prompt collections through digital-product storefronts.

Your first milestone: Create and test 15–20 prompts for one audience and one recurring task before expanding into a much larger collection.

5. Building a subscription: Turn a one-time resource into ongoing value

A subscription is not simply a digital product with a recurring payment attached.

It is an ongoing commitment to deliver something customers continue to find useful.

The fitness coach example gives us a practical starting point.

Imagine a membership called:

The Fitness Coach Resource Club

Members receive a monthly collection of resources designed to help them manage content and client communication.

Step 1: Identify a recurring need

Ask what your audience needs repeatedly rather than just once.

For example:

  • Fresh content ideas every month.
  • Updated planning templates.
  • New client communication resources.
  • Seasonal promotional materials.
  • Useful business organization tools.

A subscription makes sense only if the audience has a reason to return.

Step 2: Design the first month’s offer

Do not begin by promising an enormous resource library.

Plan a manageable first month.

Example: Month 1 deliverables

This gives the customer a clear picture of the membership.

Step 3: Use AI to plan recurring resources

Ready-to-use prompt: Monthly membership planner

Act as a digital membership product strategist.
Membership audience: [Describe audience]
Membership topic: [Topic]
Main recurring need: [Need]
Monthly delivery capacity: [Available time and resources]
Design a practical first-month resource package.
Include:
1. Three to five useful member resources.
2. The purpose of each resource.
3. What the member will receive.
4. How each resource helps solve a recurring problem.
5. A realistic production schedule.
Avoid suggesting deliverables that require
unrealistic ongoing effort.
Prioritize quality, relevance and consistency.

Use the output as a planning draft. You must decide whether you can actually deliver the proposed resources.

Step 4: Create a 12-month roadmap

A subscription needs a forward plan.

For the fitness coach membership, a simple roadmap might look like this:

This is an illustrative roadmap. You can adjust it to your audience’s actual needs and your ability to produce the material.

Step 5: Think about pricing and retention

A subscription price should reflect the value and frequency of delivery, the amount of work involved and what comparable alternatives offer.

Before setting a price, calculate:

  • Monthly production costs.
  • Platform and payment fees.
  • Time required to prepare resources.
  • Customer support requirements.
  • The number of paying members needed to cover costs.

For illustration, suppose a membership costs ₹499 per month.

If 50 customers remain subscribed for a full month, gross subscription revenue is:

50 × ₹499 = ₹24,950.

This is revenue before fees, taxes, expenses, refunds and cancellations. It is not a profit forecast or a promise of subscriber numbers.

Retention is just as important as attracting new members.

Give customers a clear onboarding experience, deliver resources when promised and make it easy to understand what they receive.

A subscription should not become a monthly folder of repetitive AI-generated content.

Step 6: Build a simple onboarding process

When someone joins, they should know:

  • What the membership includes.
  • Where to find the resources.
  • When new material will arrive.
  • How to use the resources.
  • How to get help.
  • How billing and cancellation work.

The simpler the experience, the easier it is for customers to understand the value they are paying for.

Your first milestone: Design a first-month membership package, prepare a realistic 12-month roadmap and test the offer with a small group before committing to a full launch.

A note on emerging digital products: Custom GPTs and Claude Skills

The five models above can also accommodate newer AI-based products.

For example, a digital product creator might develop:

  • A custom GPT designed to help a particular professional prepare marketing content.
  • A Claude Skill that supports a repeatable research, writing or business workflow.

These formats can potentially be packaged alongside guides, templates and other resources.

However, they require more than writing a few instructions. Their usefulness depends on how well the workflow is designed, tested and maintained. Platform availability, sharing options and commercial rules should also be checked before building an offer around them.

For now, think of them as additional product formats — not a sixth business model or a substitute for understanding customer demand.

How to choose what to build first

You have now seen five creation workflows. But which one should you actually start with?

Here is a simple comparison.

A useful starting rule:

  • Choose digital products if you enjoy creating structured resources.
  • Choose freelance services if you prefer working directly with clients.
  • Choose niche websites if you enjoy publishing and building an audience over time.
  • Choose prompt packs if you understand a specific workflow and can improve it with AI.
  • Choose subscriptions if your audience has recurring needs and you can consistently meet them.

Do not select a model simply because someone online claims it is the easiest way to earn money.

Select the one you can execute well.

Your practical 7-day build plan

To prevent this article from becoming another collection of ideas, here is a simple seven-day plan.

The schedule assumes you have already chosen an audience and validated an initial problem. Adjust it according to the complexity of your offer.

At the end of the week, you should have something tangible to review and test — not necessarily a fully launched or profitable business.

Final checklist: Is your first offer ready?

Before moving towards launch, review the following:

  • The target audience is clearly defined.
  • The problem being addressed is specific.
  • The offer has a clear purpose.
  • The deliverables are defined.
  • AI-generated material has been reviewed and improved.
  • Important claims and factual information have been checked.
  • The finished resource or service is usable.
  • The offer description accurately explains what customers receive.
  • Pricing or service scope has been considered.
  • Feedback from potential customers has been collected or planned.

If several boxes remain unchecked, do not rush to launch. Improve the offer first.

What comes next?

You have moved from an idea to a tangible offer.

But creating something useful is only half the business.

People still need to discover it, understand its value, trust the person behind it and decide to purchase.

That brings us to Part 3:

Launch, Attract Customers and Grow: A Practical Marketing and Growth Plan for Your AI-Assisted Digital Business

We will explore positioning, pricing, sales pages, organic marketing, content calendars, lead magnets, email sequences, customer acquisition, upsells, automation and performance tracking.

Because a well-built product deserves more than being uploaded to a storefront and left waiting for customers.

Build something useful. Make its value clear. Then create a system that helps the right people find it.

medium.titulo: Why Do We Even Need React, Vue and Angular? 6 Things They Do So You Don’t Have To
medium.resumo: In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself.
medium.conteudo_html:
In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself. What they add is knowing when to call them, which ones to use, and which calls to skip.

Open the source of React, Vue or Angular and you won’t find any browser magic. They create elements with document.createElement, change text with nodeValue and textContent, and attach listeners with addEventListener, exactly like you would in a plain .js file.

So why does almost every team reach for one of them? It isn’t because the DOM is slow or because vanilla JavaScript can’t build a real app. These libraries make a long list of small decisions for you, on every click, and they get them right every time. You would get most of them right too, at least on the first day. By month six, with three teammates and forty screens, you’d be getting them wrong.

Here are the six that matter most. I checked each one against the shipped source of React 19.3, Vue 3.5 and Angular 21.2, and measured the browser side in Chrome 156. The interactive version of this post, with live demos you can run in your browser, is on allahabadi.dev.

1. You stop updating the screen by hand

This is the big one, and every other point in this post sits on top of it.

Take a small shopping cart. A cart icon shows a count, a list shows the items, a line shows the total, and the checkout button says how many items you’re buying. Four places on the screen show the same piece of data.

Without a library, every action has to remember every place:

<span id="badge">0</span>
<ul id="list"></ul>
<b id="total">0</b>
<button id="checkout">Checkout (0)</button>
const cart = [];
const badge = document.querySelector('#badge');
const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const total = document.querySelector('#total');
const checkout = document.querySelector('#checkout');
function addItem(item) {
  cart.push(item);
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = `${item.name} ₹${item.price}`;
  list.append(li);
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function removeLast() {
  cart.pop();
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.lastElementChild?.remove();
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  // checkout.textContent was never updated here
}

Nothing in that code crashes. removeLast just forgets the checkout button, so after you remove an item the button still says the old number. No error shows up in the console, and no test fails unless someone wrote one for that exact label. A real app has hundreds of these "update these four things" functions, and each new feature adds one more place each of them has to remember.

The fix is to flip the direction. Instead of writing “when this happens, change these elements”, you write one function that says what the screen should look like for any cart, and you call it after every change:

let cart = [];
function render() {
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.replaceChildren(...cart.map((i) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `${i.name} ₹${i.price}`;
    return li;
  }));
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function addItem(item) { cart = [...cart, item]; render(); }
function removeLast() { cart = cart.slice(0, -1); render(); }

(It uses the same four const elements as the first snippet.) Now no action can forget the button, because no action touches the screen at all. They change the data, and render draws the screen from it. People describe this as UI is a function of state: same state in, same screen out.

That is the whole idea React, Vue and Angular are built on. In React the same cart looks like this:

import { useState } from 'react';
export function Cart() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
  const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  return (
    <>
      <span>{cart.length}</span>
      <ul>
        {cart.map((i, n) => <li key={n}>{i.name} ₹{i.price}</li>)}
      </ul>
      <b>{total}</b>
      <button onClick={() => setCart([...cart, { name: 'Tea', price: 40 }])}>Add tea</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCart(cart.slice(0, -1))}>Remove last</button>
      <button>Checkout ({cart.length})</button>
    </>
  );
}

But my vanilla render() has a cost the React version doesn't. It rebuilds the whole list on every click, even when only one item changed. Do that on a list of 2,000 rows and the browser throws away 2,000 elements and builds 2,000 new ones to change one price. Doing "render from state" without paying that price is the actual work these libraries do, and the next three sections are about how they do it.

2. They pick the right moment to touch the DOM

A browser tab runs your JavaScript and draws the page on the same thread. It can’t paint while your code is running. Roughly, one turn of the loop looks like this: run a task (your click handler), run the microtasks queued during it, run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then recalculate styles, lay the page out and paint.

When you change the DOM directly, the change happens right there, in the middle of your handler. When you then read something that depends on layout (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), innerText), the browser has to stop and lay the page out right now, because the layout it has is out of date. Do that in a loop and you get one full layout per pass. This has a name: layout thrashing.

const rows = document.querySelectorAll('.row');
const heights = [];
for (const row of rows) {
  row.textContent = 'Read';        // write: layout is now out of date
  heights.push(row.offsetHeight);  // read: browser must lay out right now
}

The libraries never write to the DOM the moment you change state. They write it down and do all the DOM work later, in one go:

  • React collects every setState call made during an event. If your click handler calls setName, setCity and setAge, React renders once and commits once, after your handler returns and before the browser paints. Work that isn't urgent, like a startTransition update, goes through React's scheduler, which posts its work with MessageChannel and gives the main thread back every 5 ms so a keypress doesn't have to wait for a long render.
  • Vue puts each component that needs updating in a queue and flushes the whole queue in one microtask (Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs)). That is why you need await nextTick() to see the updated DOM right after changing state.
  • Angular in zoneless mode schedules change detection with whichever fires first, a setTimeout or a requestAnimationFrame, so a burst of changes in one handler leads to one check.

The core of the trick fits in six lines:

let queued = false;
function scheduleRender(render) {
  if (queued) return;
  queued = true;
  queueMicrotask(() => { queued = false; render(); });
}

Call scheduleRender(render) ten times in one click and render runs once.

One correction to something you’ll often read: none of the three uses requestIdleCallback to apply your updates. An idle callback can be delayed for a long time, and an update needs to be on screen in the next frame. Vue uses it for hydrateOnIdle, and Angular for @defer (on idle) blocks. Both are cases where waiting is fine.

You can do all of this by hand. You’d have to know that layout reads in a loop are expensive, that a microtask runs before the next paint, and that requestAnimationFrame exists. Then you'd have to make sure every developer on the team knows it as well, in every file.

3. They choose the fast DOM API for you

The DOM often gives you two ways to do the same thing, and one of them costs a lot more. The best-known pair is textContent and innerText.

textContent joins up the text nodes inside an element. It never looks at CSS. innerText returns the text as it appears on screen: it leaves out elements hidden with CSS, applies text-transform, and turns line boxes into line breaks. To know what is on screen, the browser needs up-to-date styles and layout. So reading innerText right after you changed something forces a full layout.

Writing is a different story, and this is where the usual advice gets it half wrong. In my traces, setting innerText did not force layout. It cost about the same as setting textContent. The only difference is that the innerText setter turns \n into <br> elements. The expensive part is reading it.

The read is easy to put in a hot loop without noticing, like this search filter:

const query = 'error';
for (const row of document.querySelectorAll('.row')) {
  row.hidden = !row.innerText.includes(query);
}

Setting row.hidden makes the layout out of date, and the next row's innerText needs it to be current, so the browser lays the page out again for every row. Swap innerText for textContent and that loop doesn't do any layout until the frame is painted.

Here is how React sets text on an element, from react-dom 19.3 (lightly reformatted):

function setTextContent(node, text) {
  if (text) {
    var firstChild = node.firstChild;
    if (firstChild && firstChild === node.lastChild && 3 === firstChild.nodeType) {
      firstChild.nodeValue = text;
      return;
    }
  }
  node.textContent = text;
}

If the element already holds exactly one text node, React changes that node’s nodeValue in place, which is the cheapest text write the DOM has. Otherwise it uses textContent. innerText doesn't appear anywhere in that path.

Most of the time, these libraries don’t read the DOM at all. The current cart, the current name and the current filter all live in JavaScript, in React’s fibers, Vue’s reactive objects or Angular’s views. When your code reads row.innerText to find out what a row says, it asks the browser to work it out from the page. A library already knows, because it rendered that row. Fewer reads means fewer chances to force layout, and you don't need to remember which layout-reading APIs are dangerous. I measured more than 40 of them in another post.

They skip updates that change nothing

Say a price on the screen is 499, and your code sets it to 499 again. Nothing on screen changes. Does the browser notice?

I tested it in Chrome 156 on a page with 3,000 paragraphs. Each test wrote the same value 200 times and read offsetWidth after each write, the way real code often measures right after updating:

  • el.textContent = '499' (same value): 200 layouts. textContent replaces the child text node with a brand new one every time, so the browser treats it as new content.
  • el.innerHTML = '499' (same value): 200 layouts, for the same reason, plus an HTML parse each time.
  • textNode.nodeValue = '499' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome sees that nothing changed. A MutationObserver still received all 200 records, though.
  • el.style.width = '50px' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome skips an identical inline style too.
  • if (el.textContent !== '499') el.textContent = '499': 0 layouts, 0 mutations.

So the browser skips some identical writes and redoes others, and the two most common ways of setting text are the ones it redoes. You’d have to know which is which.

const price = document.querySelector('#price');
for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
  price.textContent = '499';
  price.offsetWidth;
}

All three libraries put the check in front of the DOM, so they never need that list:

  • React compares old and new text before it marks a text node for update (current.memoizedProps !== newProps). One level up, if you call setCount(5) while the count is already 5, Object.is says nothing changed and React can skip rendering that component altogether.
  • Vue’s reactive setter runs hasChanged(value, oldValue) first. Assigning the same value to a ref doesn't trigger anything that depends on it.
  • Angular compares every template binding to its previous value with Object.is (bindingUpdated) and only touches the DOM when it differs.

All three compare with Object.is, so they check "is it the same value", not "does it look the same":

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
Object.is(user, user);              // true:  update skipped
Object.is(user, { name: 'Asha' });  // false: treated as a change

That is why in React you create a new object to trigger an update, and why a new object built on every render can cause updates you didn’t expect.

5. They treat text as text

This is the reason I’d add to the list. It saves teams from a whole class of security bugs without anyone thinking about it.

When you build UI by hand, the quick way to put a value into a page is innerHTML. It parses whatever string you give it as HTML. If that string came from a user, the user can write HTML into your page, including elements with event handlers that run their JavaScript under your domain. That attack is called cross-site scripting, or XSS.

const greeting = document.querySelector('#greeting');
const name = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('name') ?? '';
greeting.innerHTML = `Hi ${name}`;    // parses name as HTML
greeting.textContent = `Hi ${name}`;  // shows name as plain text

In React, <p>Hi {name}</p> always produces a text node, whatever name holds. Vue's {{ name }} and Angular's {{ name }} work the same way. To put raw HTML on the page you have to ask for it by name: React calls it dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue calls it v-html, and Angular runs anything bound to [innerHTML] through its sanitizer first. The safe way is the default, and the unsafe way is the one you have to go looking for.

6. They make a big codebase easier to work in

The first five points are things the library does at runtime. This one is about the people writing the code, and on a large team it may matter most of all.

  • Components. A <PriceTag> is written once, used in forty places, and changed in one file. With plain DOM code, "reuse" usually means copying a function and its HTML string into another file.
  • Clean-up has a home. Listeners you attach in the template (onClick, @click, (click)) are removed for you when the component goes away, and each library gives you one obvious place for the rest: the useEffect clean-up in React, onUnmounted in Vue, DestroyRef in Angular. By hand, every removeEventListener is yours to remember, and a forgotten one keeps the old element and everything it refers to in memory.
  • Tools that understand your app. React DevTools, Vue DevTools and Angular DevTools show your components and their current state, not just a tree of divs. Hot reload swaps an edited component while the page keeps running, often without losing what you typed into a form.
  • The editor catches mistakes. TypeScript checks JSX and Angular templates, so a misspelled prop or a wrong type shows up as you type, not as a blank screen.
  • A shared map. Routing, forms, data fetching and tests have well-known answers in each ecosystem. A new teammate who knows React already knows where state lives in your app and how a screen gets drawn. Hand-written DOM code is different in every company, and sometimes in every file.

When plain JavaScript is enough

None of this means every page needs a framework. This site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework at all. A blog post, a landing page, or a form with a couple of toggles has very little state and only a few places that show it, so the bugs from the first section rarely have room to happen.

A simple rule of thumb: reach for a library when the same data shows up in several parts of the screen and changes often. That’s where updating by hand starts to break, and where batching, skipping and safe defaults pay for the JavaScript you ship. Below that point, a few addEventListener calls and textContent are perfectly fine.

React, Vue and Angular are still DOM code. They call the same APIs you can. The difference is that they pick the moment, pick the cheap method, skip the pointless call and escape the dangerous string on every update, including the ones nobody on your team thought about.

All five demos (the two carts, the batching race, the innerText filter, the same-value counter and the innerHTML parser) run live here: https://allahabadi.dev/blogs/frontend/why-we-need-react-vue-angular/

medium.conteudo_html:
只要在 pages/ 資料夾裡面新增一個 .vue 檔案

Nuxt 就能自動產生對應的頁面路由

以前學 Vue 或 Angular 時，多少都有接觸過路由設定

但 Nuxt 這種方式讓我覺得很不一樣

為什麼只是新增一個檔案，Nuxt 就知道它對應哪個網址

什麼是 Routing

Routing（路由），簡單來說，就是決定使用者進入某個網址時，應該顯示哪個頁面。

一個電影網站：

  • /：首頁
  • /movies：電影列表
  • /about：關於我們

一般使用 Vue Router 時，我們可以自行設定網址與 Component 的對應關係。

const routes = [
  {
    path: '/movies',
    component: MovieList
  }
]

意思是當使用者進入 /movies，就顯示 MovieList 這個元件。

但 Nuxt 幫我們省去了許多手動設定的工作。

Nuxt 的檔案式路由

Nuxt 有一個功能叫做 File-based Routing 檔案式路由

只要在 pages/ 裡面建立對應的 Vue 檔案

就能依照檔案結構自動建立路由

pages/
  index.vue
  about.vue
  movies/
    index.vue
    popular.vue

Nuxt 會依照預設規則產生：

pages/index.vue
就是 /

pages/about.vue
就是 /about

pages/movies/index.vue
就是 /movies

pages/movies/popular.vue
就是 /movies/popular

Nuxt 不是每次有人輸入網址，才去資料夾裡尋找檔案

而是在開發或建置應用程式時，掃描 pages/ 裡面的檔案，依照命名規則自動產生 Vue Router 的路由設定

所以我們不用每新增一個頁面，就自己寫一次路由對照表

index.vue 代表該層路徑的預設頁面

因此 pages/index.vue 對應 /

而 pages/movies/index.vue 對應 /movies

網址裡面的內容會改變

假設電影網站有幾千部電影

難道要為每部電影建立一個 Vue 檔案嗎？

當然不用。

Nuxt 提供了 Dynamic Routes 動態路由。

pages/
  movies/
    index.vue
    [id].vue

其中 [id].vue 的 id 是一個可以變動的路由參數。

因此以下網址，都能對應到同一個頁面元件：

/movies/100
/movies/200
/movies/300

那要怎麼知道使用者目前選擇哪部電影？

可以使用 useRoute()：

<script setup>
const route = useRoute()
const movieId = route.params.id
</script>

<template>
  <h1>電影編號：{{ movieId }}</h1>
</template>

假設使用者進入：

/movies/100

那麼 route.params.id 就會取得 "100"。

之後就可以根據這個 ID，向 API 查詢對應的電影資料。

路由負責決定顯示哪個頁面，以及提供網址參數

但不代表它會自動幫我們查詢資料。

NuxtPage 又是做什麼

了解路由怎麼產生後，還有一個問題。

Nuxt 知道 /movies 對應哪個頁面，但它要把頁面顯示在哪裡？

這時就會用到 <NuxtPage />。

例如在 app.vue 中：

<template>
  <NuxtPage />
</template>

可以把它想成一個放置目前頁面的容器。

當使用者進入 /movies，Nuxt Router 就會根據路由設定，讓對應的頁面元件顯示在這個位置。

如果想要在網站裡切換頁面，也可以使用 Nuxt 提供的 <NuxtLink>：

<NuxtLink to="/movies">
  查看電影列表
</NuxtLink>

點擊後，就能在應用程式中導向電影列表頁面。

重點整理

  • Routing（路由）：決定網址要對應哪個頁面。
  • File-based Routing（檔案式路由）：Nuxt 根據 pages/ 的檔案結構，自動產生路由設定。
  • index.vue：代表該資料夾層級的預設頁面。
  • Dynamic Routes（動態路由）：使用 [id].vue 等檔名，讓不同的網址參數共用同一個頁面元件。
  • useRoute()：取得目前的路由資訊，例如網址參數。
  • NuxtPage：顯示目前路由對應的頁面元件。
  • NuxtLink：在 Nuxt 應用程式中進行頁面導航。

流程

  • Nuxt 掃描 pages/
  • 自動產生路由設定
  • Vue Router 比對網址
  • NuxtPage 顯示對應的頁面

corrida_no_ar.titulo: R$ 6,5 MIL em um TÊNIS! O preço IMPRESSIONANTE do Adios Pro EVO 3
corrida_no_ar.resumo: O Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3 chega ao Brasil por R$ 6,5 mil. Confira os favoritos para a Maratona de Nova York, os detalhes da Maratona de Aracaju, o calendário do Mountain Do e as datas da Meia e Maratona de Buenos Aires 2027.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sexta-feira | 30 de outubro de 2026

O tênis usado para correr a maratona abaixo de 2 horas e bater o recorde mundial da meia maratona, o Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3, acaba de ser lançado no Brasil com um preço que está dando o que falar: a bagatela de R$ 6.499,99. O valor é tão surreal que com a mesma quantia seria possível comprar três pares do Adios Pro 5. A novidade já está disponível no site da Adidas, mas o preço exorbitante levanta a questão de até quando valores como esse serão normalizados no mercado.

Quem são os favoritos para a Maratona de Nova York?

Neste domingo, acontece a Maratona de Nova York, e a disputa promete ser acirrada. No masculino, o grande favorito é o queniano Benson Kipruto, que já venceu a prova, é um atleta muito regular e conhece bem o percurso desafiador da cidade. No entanto, muitos estão de olho na estreia do sueco Andreas Almgren, recordista europeu da meia maratona e atual campeão mundial da distância. Apesar de sua estreia, Almgren se mostrou confiante, embora a prova de Nova York nivele a competição e não perdoe erros. Vale lembrar que um europeu nascido na Europa não vence a prova desde 1996.

Entre as mulheres, o favoritismo se concentra em duas atletas: Hellen Obiri, bicampeã da maratona, que busca o tricampeonato para se juntar a lendas como Grete Waitz e Paula Radcliffe, e a vencedora do ano passado, Sheila Chepkirui. A disputa entre as duas promete ser o ponto alto da prova feminina.

Última etapa do ASICS Run Challenge em Florianópolis

O ASICS Run Challenge chega à sua última etapa no dia 8 de novembro, em Florianópolis. O evento, que já passou por Belo Horizonte, Brasília, Fortaleza, Salvador e Recife, oferece percursos de 4k, 7k e 15k. Se você quiser participar, pode usar o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 para garantir 10% de desconto na inscrição.

Maratona de Aracaju: números e previsão do tempo

A Maratona de Aracaju, que acontece neste fim de semana, divulgou seus números de inscritos. Serão 4,5 mil atletas nos 5k, 3 mil nos 10k, 6 mil nos 21k e 2,5 mil nos 42k, além de 350 atletas no desafio de 63k. Com esses números, a prova disputa o posto de maior maratona do Nordeste com a de Fortaleza. Quem estiver por lá, pode visitar o estande do Brasil Gigante na feira do evento para pegar adesivos e conferir os produtos exclusivos.

A previsão do tempo, segundo o site especializado Artrak, é de um clima desafiador. A temperatura deve ficar entre 25°C e 30°C, com sensação de ar abafado e alta radiação solar. A chuva é improvável, mas o vento será de leve a moderado. O estresse térmico será alto, com impacto moderado a alto no desempenho, especialmente para quem vai correr os 21k e 42k. Portanto, a recomendação é ter muito cuidado com a hidratação e não subestimar o calor.

Mountain Do 2027 com desconto exclusivo

O calendário de 2027 do Mountain Do já está no ar, com etapas em locais incríveis como Praia do Rosa (SC), Deserto da Namíbia, Chapada dos Veadeiros (GO), Fim do Mundo (Argentina), Fernando de Noronha, Selva Amazônica, Deserto do Saara (Marrocos) e Pantanal. Para quem quer garantir sua vaga, o Corrida no Ar oferece um cupom exclusivo: CORRIDANOAR10, que dá 10% de desconto nas inscrições.

Buenos Aires anuncia datas para 2027

De forma inédita e com muita antecedência, a organização da Meia e da Maratona de Buenos Aires já anunciou as datas para as provas de 2027. A Meia Maratona acontecerá no dia 22 de agosto, enquanto a Maratona será realizada no dia 19 de setembro. As inscrições devem abrir em breve, então fique atento para não perder a oportunidade de correr uma das provas mais queridas pelos brasileiros.
